title: Death Threats & Breach of Peace in Bangladesh: Section 107 CrPC Peace Bond Guide
metaTitle: Section 107 CrPC Peace Bond: Executive Magistrate Court BD
metaDescription: Facing death threats or violent neighbor disputes in Bangladesh? Learn how to file a Section 107 CrPC peace bond case in Executive Magistrate Court.
keywords: neighbor boundary dispute life threat bangladesh
heroIntro: A common and alarming situation arises across Bangladesh: following an unresolved boundary dispute, family inheritance squabble, tenancy confrontation, or political disagreement, an aggressive neighbor, relative, or local hoodlum begins issuing overt death threats (Pran Nasher Humki). They shout abuse, threaten to break limbs, vandalize your property, or assemble armed thugs outside your gate. When you visit the local police station to report the terror, the duty officer often advises: 'This is a non-cognizable civil dispute; file a General Diary (GD).' However, a standard GD does not arrest the aggressor or provide physical protection. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, the law provides a swift, preventative criminal judicial remedy: filing a proceeding under Section 107 of the CrPC before the Executive Magistrate Court to bind the aggressor down under a Peace Bond (Muchleka) with heavy sureties.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: How Can You Legally Stop Death Threats and Intimidation in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC), whenever an Executive Magistrate receives information that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb public tranquility, or to do any wrongful act that may occasion a breach of the peace, the Magistrate can issue a summons requiring that person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a Peace Bond (Muchleka), with or without sureties, for keeping the peace for up to one (1) year. To stop imminent threats immediately, the victim's advocate can petition under Section 117(3) CrPC for an emergency Interim Security Bond. If the aggressor refuses to execute the bond, violates its conditions, or repeats threats, the Magistrate can immediately remand them to central jail under Section 122 CrPC.
highlights: Section 107 CrPC empowers Executive Magistrates to restrain aggressive individuals issuing death threats.
Under Section 117(3) CrPC, the Magistrate can compel an immediate Interim Peace Bond during inquiry.
The court requires the aggressor to submit financial sureties and sworn commitments not to approach the victim.
Breaching a peace bond results in immediate forfeiture of financial sureties and jail detention under Section 122.
points: Step 1: Lodge a detailed General Diary (GD) at the local Thana documenting the exact threats, dates, and witnesses.
Step 2: Collect audio recordings of phone threats, CCTV footage, and eyewitness corroboration.
Step 3: File a formal Petition under Section 107 CrPC before the Executive Magistrate Court (District/Upazila).
Step 4: Move an emergency petition under Section 117(3) CrPC for immediate interim peace bond execution.

sections.title: The Reality of Threats and Intimidation in Bangladesh
sections.content:
In Bangladesh's crowded neighborhoods and semi-urban commercial centers, disputes over property boundaries, shop rentals, family partitions, or personal rivalries often cross the line from civil disagreements into open terror. Unscrupulous parties frequently hire local musclemen or assemble gangs to intimidate peaceable families. They issue explicit death threats, warn victims that their children will be harmed, and threaten to dismantle boundary fences at night.

Victims who rush to the local police station frequently encounter procedural inertia: because verbal threats (criminal intimidation under Section 506 of the Penal Code) are technically classified as non-cognizable offenses, the police cannot arrest the aggressor without a court order, merely recording an entry in the General Diary (GD). Relying solely on a passive GD leaves the family in acute physical danger. The Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 anticipated this exact administrative vacuum, providing a powerful preventative weapon under Section 107 before actual bloodshed occurs.

sections.title: Understanding Preventive Criminal Justice: Section 107 CrPC
sections.content:
Criminal jurisprudence in Bangladesh is divided into punitive justice (punishing crimes after they occur) and preventative justice (stopping crimes before they happen). Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC) is the cornerstone of preventative criminal administration.

Section 107(1) stipulates: 'Whenever an Executive Magistrate is informed that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquility, or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion a breach of the peace, the Magistrate may... require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace for such period not exceeding one year as the Magistrate thinks fit to fix.' This provision does not aim to brand the aggressor as a convicted criminal; its objective is to place a heavy judicial leash around their neck, compelling them to furnish substantial financial sureties that will be immediately forfeited if they misbehave.

sections.title: Role and Jurisdiction of the Executive Magistrate Court
sections.content:
Following the historic separation of the judiciary from the executive in 2007 (the Masdar Hossain case), judicial powers under the CrPC were divided between Judicial Magistrates and Executive Magistrates. While Judicial Magistrates conduct criminal trials, the maintenance of public order, breach of peace, and preventative security under Sections 107, 144, and 145 CrPC are assigned exclusively to Executive Magistrates.

In Dhaka, Chattogram, and metropolitan areas, Executive Magistrate Courts operate under the District Administration (headed by the District Magistrate / Deputy Commissioner) or specialized Metropolitan Executive Magistrate benches. In upazilas, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) or Assistant Commissioner (Land) functions as an Executive Magistrate. These courts possess summary authority to summon parties, direct the local Thana police to submit expedited inquiry reports, and issue binding orders maintaining peace.

sections.title: Section 117: Interim Peace Bonds for Urgent Protection
sections.content:
The standard inquiry under Section 107 requires examining witnesses, which can take several weeks. If the victim faces imminent threat of physical violence tonight, waiting for the final order offers little solace. To solve this emergency, the legislature enacted Section 117(3) of the CrPC.

Section 117(3) provides an extraordinary emergency remedy: 'The Magistrate may, if he considers that immediate measures are necessary for the prevention of a breach of the peace or disturbance of the public tranquility or the commission of any offence or for the public safety, for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person in respect of whom the order under section 112 has been made to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour until the conclusion of the inquiry, and may detain him in custody until such bond is executed.' An advocate files an emergency interlocutory application under Section 117(3) alongside the main petition, securing an immediate interim bond on the very first day of appearance.

sections.title: Police Inquiry Reports and Thana Investigation Protocols
sections.content:
Upon receiving a petition under Section 107 CrPC, the Executive Magistrate issues an official order directing the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the local Thana to depute a Sub-Inspector (SI) to conduct an on-site field inquiry. The police officer visits the disputed locality, interviews neighbors, examines boundary lines, and inspects recorded General Diaries.

The police officer then prepares a formal Police Inquiry Report submitted directly to the Executive Magistrate Court. If the report confirms that the opposite party is aggressive, maintains armed associates, and that an imminent breach of the peace exists, the Magistrate immediately issues a Show Cause Order under Section 112 CrPC. This official police verification strips the aggressor of any plausible deniability, compelling the court to demand high financial sureties.

sections.title: Consequences of Violating a Bond: Forfeiture and Jail
sections.content:
A Peace Bond executed under Section 107 CrPC is not a hollow piece of paper; it carries severe financial and physical penalties. When an aggressor executes a bond, they must submit personal recognizance alongside two reputable local sureties (such as solvent business owners or municipal councillors) who pledge substantial financial sums (typically BDT 50,000 to BDT 2,00,000 each).

Under Section 122 and Section 514 of the CrPC, if the bound person violates the peace during the one-year bond period—by uttering fresh death threats, assaulting the complainant, or trespassing on their land—the consequences are swift:

  1. Immediate Forfeiture of Money: The Magistrate passes a summary order forfeiting the entire bond amount. If the sureties fail to pay, the court attaches and sells their immovable property through public distress warrants.
  2. Remand to Jail Custody: Under Section 123 CrPC, if the aggressor refuses to execute the bond or breaches the peace, the Magistrate orders the offender remanded directly to central jail for the entire unexpired duration of the bond period.

sections.title: Combining Section 107 with Penal Code Section 506
sections.content:
To build an impenetrable legal defense, an experienced criminal advocate adopts a two-pronged strategy: combining preventative administrative proceedings with formal criminal prosecution. Parallel to the Section 107 petition before the Executive Magistrate Court, the advocate files a Complaint Register (CR) case under Section 506 of the Penal Code 1860 (Criminal Intimidation) before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) Court.

Under the second part of Section 506, if the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, or to cause the destruction of any property by fire, the offense is punishable with imprisonment for up to seven (7) years, or with fine, or with both. Prosecuting under Section 506 alongside Section 107 exposes the aggressor to long-term criminal prison sentences while simultaneously binding them under an immediate peace bond, completely disarming their aggressive posture.

sections.title: Comparison Table: General Diary (GD) vs. Section 107 CrPC
sections.content:
The table below summarizes the operational differences between relying solely on a police General Diary versus pursuing a Section 107 CrPC court proceeding:

ParameterPolice General Diary (GD) AloneSection 107 CrPC Court Case
Judicial AuthorityNone; purely an internal police station logJudicial proceeding before Executive Magistrate
Power to Compel OpponentNone; police cannot compel appearanceCourt summons & non-bailable warrants
Financial SuretiesZero financial deterrenceSurety bonds of BDT 50,000–2,00,000
Jail Detention PowerNone without registering formal FIRDirect imprisonment under §123 for non-compliance
Speed of ReliefPassive; often archived without actionInterim peace bond under §117(3) within days

A General Diary merely records an allegation; a Section 107 court case enforces immediate legal deterrence that restrains aggressive opponents.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Stopping a Land Grabber's Threats in Mirpur
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an emergency Section 107 proceeding neutralized a violent threat in Mirpur, Dhaka:

A retired government school headmaster lived in a modest residential house in Mirpur-12, Dhaka. An influential local real estate developer purchased an adjacent plot and demanded that the headmaster sell his front driveway at a nominal price to allow road widening for a commercial building. When the headmaster refused, the developer sent armed thugs who banged on his iron gates at night, shouted obscenities, and verbally warned him that if he did not sign a deed within seven days, 'his body would be found floating in the Turag River.' The terrified family lodged two GDs at Pallabi Thana, but the threats only escalated.

The headmaster consulted a criminal defense advocate. The advocate drafted an urgent petition under Section 107 of the CrPC, filed directly in the Court of the Executive Magistrate, Dhaka, accompanied by an interlocutory petition under Section 117(3) for an interim peace bond. The petition annexed the two stamped GD entries, audio recordings of telephone threats, and photographs of the developer's associates outside the gate.

The Executive Magistrate took immediate cognizance, issued a Show Cause Notice under Section 112 CrPC, and directed the Officer-in-Charge of Pallabi Thana to submit an expedited inquiry report within three days. The police visited the site, warned the developer, and confirmed the threat to the Magistrate. On the return date, the Magistrate ordered the developer to execute an immediate Interim Peace Bond of BDT 1,00,000 with two solvent local sureties, warning him that any further harassment would result in immediate remand to Dhaka Central Jail. Confronted with immediate imprisonment and financial forfeiture, the developer dismissed his thugs and abandoned his unlawful demands, restoring complete peace to the family.

faqs.question: What is Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Section 107 CrPC is a preventative criminal law provision that empowers Executive Magistrates to order any person who threatens a breach of the peace or public tranquility to execute a Peace Bond (Muchleka), with financial sureties, for keeping the peace for up to one year.

faqs.question: Which court handles Section 107 cases in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Section 107 proceedings are heard exclusively by Executive Magistrate Courts operating under the District Administration in metropolitan cities and district headquarters, or by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) in upazila jurisdictions.

faqs.question: Is filing a General Diary (GD) enough to stop death threats?
faqs.answer: No. A General Diary is merely an administrative record in the police register. To legally force the aggressor to stop threats under threat of imprisonment and financial forfeiture, you must file a formal case under Section 107 CrPC before the Executive Magistrate.

faqs.question: What is an Interim Peace Bond under Section 117(3) CrPC?
faqs.answer: An Interim Peace Bond is an emergency order granted by the Magistrate at the initial stage of the proceeding, requiring the aggressor to immediately sign a financial bond keeping the peace while the full inquiry is ongoing.

faqs.question: What happens if a person violates a Section 107 Peace Bond?
faqs.answer: Under Section 122 and Section 514 CrPC, the court will forfeit the entire bond money, attach the properties of the sureties, and remand the offender directly to central jail under Section 123 for the remaining bond period.

faqs.question: Can Section 107 be used in neighbor boundary or land disputes?
faqs.answer: Yes. When land or boundary disputes escalate into verbal death threats, physical intimidation, or assembling armed men, Section 107 is the standard legal mechanism to maintain the peace while civil title suits proceed.

faqs.question: Can an accused person be jailed under Section 107 CrPC?
faqs.answer: While Section 107 is preventative rather than punitive, if the summoned person refuses to execute the required peace bond or violates its conditions, the Magistrate has full statutory authority to order them detained in jail.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a Section 107 case for family safety in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB can execute a Power of Attorney or authorize family members residing in Bangladesh to institute Section 107 proceedings through an advocate to protect elderly parents and ancestral homes from local intimidation.
